items.title: Cloudflare launches new AI traffic management options with nuanced controls for search, agent, and training bots to help website owners protect content and optimize access [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cloudflare's new AI traffic options for customers
items.summary:
Cloudflare has introduced new AI-driven traffic management features that allow website owners to better control and monetize access to their content. These options classify AI traffic into three categories—search, agent, and training bots—enabling more precise management beyond simply blocking all AI automation.

The update reflects evolving concerns about AI bots using website content without compensation and the need for more nuanced solutions that balance content protection with discoverability. Cloudflare encourages bot operators to separate their crawlers by purpose to increase transparency and help site owners manage access according to the specific AI use case.

items.title: Anthropic updates context engineering for Claude 5 models, cutting over 80% of system prompt in Claude Code with no loss in coding performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
items.summary: Anthropic has revised its approach to context engineering for its Claude 5 generation models, significantly reducing the system prompt content in Claude Code by more than 80% without measurable impact on coding evaluation results. The company found that earlier constraints and detailed instructions were often redundant as newer models demonstrate improved judgment and can interpret user intent more effectively. This update reflects a shift from rigid rules and examples toward more flexible, interface-driven context design and progressive disclosure of information. The changes aim to optimize how context is assembled from various sources like system prompts, skills, and memory, enhancing Claude's ability to handle diverse user prompts and tasks more naturally.

items.title: Developer runs a 28.9 million parameter language model on an $8 ESP32-S3 microcontroller using Per-Layer Embeddings to fit most parameters in flash memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Running a 28.9M parameter LLM on an $8 microcontroller
items.summary:
A developer has implemented a 28.9 million parameter language model that runs entirely on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller costing about $8, generating text at roughly 9 tokens per second on a small attached screen. This model is about 100 times larger than previous models run on similar chips, achieved by storing most parameters in slow flash memory and loading only small portions into fast SRAM as needed, using a technique inspired by Google's Per-Layer Embeddings from the Gemma models.

The model was trained on the TinyStories dataset to generate short, simple stories and does not support complex tasks like question answering or code generation due to its limited reasoning capacity. The project includes firmware, wiring instructions, and training code available on GitHub, demonstrating a novel approach to fitting large language models on resource-constrained microcontrollers.

items.title: DOE announces first 278 projects under Genesis Mission to accelerate AI-driven scientific discovery across energy, science, and national security [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DOE announces first Genesis Mission projects for AI-driven scientific discovery
items.summary:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has selected 278 projects as part of its Genesis Mission to develop AI-enabled scientific workflows aimed at accelerating breakthroughs in energy, discovery science, and national security. These projects involve 342 institutions, including national laboratories, universities, companies, and nonprofits, and represent the largest response to a DOE funding opportunity in history.

The largest award is a $60 million, three-year investment in nuclear energy to use AI for faster, safer, and more cost-effective nuclear facility development. Selected teams will access the Genesis Mission Platform, which includes AI frameworks, advanced models, and high-performance computing resources to enhance research productivity and innovation across DOE mission areas.

items.title: Research finds 30 unguarded consequential actions in 25 AI agent frameworks after scanning 23,476 files for model-controlled parameters without authorization checks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: I scanned my AI agent framework for destructive/consequential actions, and wow
items.summary:
A study scanned 25 AI agent frameworks comprising 23,476 files to identify cases where a model-controlled parameter could trigger consequential actions without proper authorization checks. The scan found 30 such cases, highlighting a gap between validation and authorization in AI agent tools. The research also identified and fixed 12 false positives in its scanning process before publishing the results.

The study emphasized that most agent tools verify request format but often lack checks ensuring the caller's permission at the point of action. The scanner focused on detecting paths where no dominating authorization check exists before a consequential action occurs. The research included non-agent repositories to measure precision and improved detection rules to reduce false positives. The scanner runs locally without runtime dependencies or network calls, providing quick analysis of codebases for potential authorization gaps in AI agents.

items.title: NYU Stern expert says AI-driven memory chip shortages are causing hidden price increases in upcoming smartphones
items.originalTitle: NYU Stern pricing expert: The hidden 'AI tax' hitting your next phone
items.summary:
An NYU Stern pricing expert explains that the rising costs of memory chips, driven by increased demand from AI data centers for high-bandwidth memory, are leading to higher prices for consumer electronics like smartphones. This supply constraint, combined with manufacturers' strategies to run AI models directly on devices, is pushing up production costs that are passed on to consumers.

The shortage results from chip manufacturers allocating more capacity to higher-margin AI memory chips, reducing availability for conventional memory used in phones and laptops. Apple and other PC makers have already raised prices due to these supply issues, with analysts expecting continued price increases and constrained device shipments throughout 2026. This dynamic highlights how operational factors in semiconductor supply chains are influencing consumer electronics pricing beyond traditional demand considerations.

The discussion underscores the evolving landscape of AI-assisted software development, where leveraging large language models requires careful validation and robust testing frameworks to ensure code reliability and effectiveness.

items.originalTitle: The hidden cost of AI: Why your town is negotiating with Amazon and Microsoft
items.summary:
Local governments across the U.S. are negotiating agreements with major tech companies like Amazon and Microsoft to host AI data centers, securing significant community investments in exchange for accommodating the facilities. These deals often include funding for public services, schools, and housing, aiming to offset the increased energy demand and infrastructure strain caused by the data centers.

The negotiations have become complex as utilities and towns seek to balance the economic benefits with the rising electricity costs linked to data center growth, which PJM market monitors estimate could add $23 billion in expenses through 2028. Some communities have faced backlash over opaque deal-making, leading to political upheaval and project delays, while new regulatory measures and utility policies are encouraging data centers to finance their own energy capacity to reduce the burden on existing ratepayers.

items.originalTitle: Show HN: Rules that stop AI coding agents from breaking working code
items.summary:
A new set of rules and prompts has been published on GitHub to help AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex avoid breaking existing working code during modifications. These guidelines focus on constraints and structured prompts to improve reliability by requiring plans before changes, verification through tests, and clear boundaries on what files can be modified.

The rules include creating a project-specific file that the AI reads at the start of each session, enforcing prohibitions rather than vague requests, and strategies like saving and restoring code states to make changes reversible. The approach addresses issues caused by growing codebases and context rot in long AI sessions, aiming to reduce collateral damage and repeated mistakes by the AI agents.

items.title: MIT installs over 500 AI surveillance cameras across campus with real-time face and object classification, spending $3 million through September 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MIT to become hotbed of AI video surveillance
items.summary:
MIT is deploying more than 500 AI-powered surveillance cameras in academic buildings, residence halls, and outdoor areas along Memorial Drive, with installation ongoing since November 2025 and expected to continue until September 2026. The cameras, part of Hanwha's Wisenet AI line, can detect motion, loitering, crowds, face masks, and tampering, and classify individuals by clothing color, gender, and age up to 35 feet away. Data collected is retained for up to 30 days unless exceptions apply.

The cameras support resolutions from 2MP to 4K and feature pan, tilt, rotate, and zoom capabilities, monitored continuously by AI software Ai-RGUS. This initiative represents a significant investment in AI surveillance technology on campus, raising questions about privacy and monitoring practices.

items.title: David Mumford explores the need for AI systems to possess agency to act and collaborate in the real world, analyzing human cognitive development and current AI limitations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AIs and Humans with Agency by David Mumford
items.summary:
David Mumford discusses the transformation needed for artificial intelligence systems, particularly large language models, to gain agency—the ability to act and make decisions in the real world alongside humans. He argues that current AI lacks real-world understanding and emotions, limiting their capacity to collaborate and plan with people effectively.

Mumford draws parallels between AI and human brain function, referencing psychological and neurological studies on human skill acquisition and collaboration. He reviews early AI attempts to incorporate agency, including robotics and recent AI models, and proposes a complex multi-headed AI architecture to support integration into business environments, noting this remains a significant and challenging project with potential societal pushback.

items.originalTitle: Monday.com is the latest tech company to blame AI for layoffs — here are 20 others
items.summary:
Monday.com announced plans to lay off about 20% of its workforce, over 600 employees, as part of a restructuring tied to its AI-driven growth strategy. The company emphasized the cuts support a leaner operating model aligned with its AI-first vision rather than direct cost reduction or AI replacing jobs.

This move reflects a broader trend in the tech industry, where major companies including Microsoft, Oracle, and Google have cited AI as a factor in workforce reductions while simultaneously investing heavily in AI infrastructure and hiring for AI-focused roles. Despite these layoffs, some AI-centric firms like Anthropic and OpenAI are expanding rapidly, and some companies are shifting headcount toward AI roles rather than eliminating it entirely.

items.title: Harvard professor outlines a 'work versus gym' framework to decide when AI should be used for tasks, emphasizing process importance in skill development [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Should you use AI for a task? Here's a simple way to decide
items.summary:
A Harvard Kennedy School professor proposes a simple method to determine when AI should be used for tasks, distinguishing between 'work' tasks that prioritize output and 'gym' tasks where the process is crucial for skill building. The framework suggests using AI for tasks that must be done regardless of how, but avoiding AI for tasks where the learning process matters, such as writing assignments designed to develop critical thinking.

The professor explains that while AI can reliably handle routine or technical writing, tasks aimed at developing human skills require active engagement without AI assistance. This distinction also applies to creative fields, where some outputs are purely functional and others are artistic, affecting the role of human creators versus AI. The approach helps clarify when AI integration is appropriate and when it might hinder personal or professional growth.

items.title: Axtary launches content authorization tool for AI agents to enforce precise action approvals and enhance security in engineering and agent operations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Axtary – Content Authorization for AI Agents
items.summary:
Axtary introduces a content authorization system for AI agents that verifies exact payloads before execution, requiring human approval for higher-risk actions and recording all attempts in a ledger. The tool governs sensitive operations such as code changes, data access, and messaging, enforcing policies locally to keep provider credentials secure.

The system uses ActionPass to bind human approval to specific payload hashes, preventing unauthorized changes after review. It integrates with existing runtimes and connectors, coordinating team policies and approvals through a hosted control plane while keeping enforcement and credentials local. Axtary aims to improve security and compliance in AI-driven workflows by limiting agent authority to approved actions only.

items.title: Isomorphic Labs launches IsoDDE AI system that designs drug candidates in seconds but efficacy in clinical trials remains unproven [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Can Now Design Drugs in Seconds; We Still Can't Tell You If They Work
items.summary:
Isomorphic Labs, a Google DeepMind spinoff, released IsoDDE, an AI-driven drug design engine that rapidly predicts protein structures and ligand binding, significantly speeding up early-stage drug discovery. Despite partnerships with major pharma companies like Eli Lilly, Novartis, and Johnson & Johnson, no AI-discovered drug has yet received FDA approval, and the system's ability to predict drug efficacy in patients remains uncertain.

IsoDDE outperforms previous models in computational benchmarks, but AI-designed drugs still face a critical challenge in Phase II clinical trials, where efficacy is tested; success rates remain similar to traditional methods. While AI improves safety and pharmacokinetics predictions, its impact on overall drug development success is incremental rather than revolutionary, with more conclusive results expected as Isomorphic's candidates enter trials in late 2026.

items.title: Yes-Brainer app enables multiple large language models to deliberate and reach consensus on complex questions through parallel, trial, and consensus modes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multiple LLMs trying to reach a consensus
items.summary:
Researchers developed Yes-Brainer, an app that sends a question to multiple large language models (LLMs) simultaneously and facilitates their deliberation to improve decision-making accuracy. The app supports three modes: Parallel, where models provide independent answers; Trial, where models anonymously vote on each other's responses before a judge synthesizes a verdict; and Consensus, which involves multi-round debates mediated to reach agreement or highlight disagreements.

Yes-Brainer allows mixing models from various providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others, each retaining their native capabilities such as web search and code execution. The app aims to leverage diverse model perspectives to increase confidence in AI-generated outputs, especially for complex or important questions where single-model answers may vary significantly.
items.description:

items.summary:
Libraries across the US are offering 'Avoiding AI' workshops that guide attendees through disabling AI tools on popular devices and platforms, responding to widespread frustration with AI features being imposed without consent. The workshops, inspired by a librarian in Maine and replicated by others including one in Philadelphia, have attracted unprecedented interest, with some sessions reaching over 70 participants and generating significant social media engagement.

The sessions begin with explanations of how AI chatbots and consumer AI tools work, followed by step-by-step instructions on turning off AI features. Organizers emphasize digital literacy and user autonomy, addressing concerns about forced AI adoption and its broader implications. Attendees share tips and express mixed views, appreciating AI's benefits in areas like medicine while opposing its pervasive, involuntary presence in daily technology use.

items.title: Power line failure near Washington, DC triggered 3.1 GW data center load drop, causing grid instability across PJM region [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: One fallen power line exposed a growing AI data center problem. Here’s how to fix it.
items.summary:
A fallen power line outside Washington, DC caused over 3 gigawatts of data centers in Northern Virginia to simultaneously disconnect from the PJM grid, leading to voltage spikes and flickering lights from Northern Virginia to Chicago. This event revealed how data centers' rapid switch to backup power can destabilize the grid, highlighting a growing challenge as data center density increases in the region.

The incident lasted over 10 minutes before the grid stabilized, with data centers representing about 3% of PJM's total demand at the time. Experts say the near-simultaneous disconnection of large loads exacerbates grid fluctuations, and call for more coordinated or resilient data center power management. Startups like ON.Energy are developing systems that use battery banks and power conversion to smooth data center loads and absorb grid disruptions, aiming to prevent future large-scale disconnections and improve grid stability.

items.title: AI companies buy and destroy rare physical books to train language models, exploiting first-sale doctrine and keeping purchases anonymous [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Companies Are Buying Antique Books, Ingesting Their Contents to Train Models, and Then Destroying Them at Incredible Scale
items.summary:
AI companies are purchasing large quantities of antique and rare physical books, scanning their contents to train large language models, and then destroying the books. This practice leverages the first-sale doctrine, allowing buyers to digitize and transform the books without copyright infringement, a legal interpretation upheld in a recent lawsuit involving Anthropic. Book sellers and services like ISBNdb facilitate these bulk purchases, often keeping the buyers anonymous to avoid negative publicity.

The trend has led to a surge in sales of rare and out-of-print books, raising concerns among booksellers about the loss of unique physical copies. While some sellers benefit financially from clearing old inventory, others express unease about the destruction of culturally valuable materials. The practice is becoming widespread enough that it is impacting rare book markets in multiple countries, though the exact buyers are often speculative due to confidentiality measures.

items.title: Conservative candidates use AI-generated deepfake ads in local US elections, raising concerns about voter manipulation and misinformation [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Voters Are Being Inundated by a Barrage of AI-Generated Election Ads
items.summary:
AI-generated deepfake ads are increasingly used in US local elections, with conservative candidates deploying manipulated videos to attack rivals and influence voters. In St. Charles, Missouri, candidate Jason Law aired AI-created ads portraying opponents in a negative light, while similar tactics appeared in races in California and Kentucky. These ads often feature synthetic voices and fabricated scenarios, complicating voters' ability to discern truth from fiction.

The use of AI in political advertising has sparked criticism, including from targeted candidates who argue that older voters may be particularly vulnerable to deception due to unfamiliarity with AI technology. Independent political action committees have also funded such ads, contributing to a growing trend of AI-driven misinformation in electoral campaigns. The impact of these ads is evident in election outcomes, as seen in the Kentucky congressional race where AI ads coincided with a challenger’s victory.

The app can narrate stories with either a human or AI voice and aims to help exhausted parents provide unique stories quickly.

StoryKit is currently in testing in select countries and is not yet available in the US. Meta positions the app as a way to reduce parental guilt over screen time by offering AI-generated stories, though some critics question whether this replaces valuable parent-child bonding moments traditionally fostered through storytelling.

items.title: OpenAI launches Micro AI keypad for ChatGPT with customizable keys and voice dictation, targeting coders but receiving mixed reviews [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: I tried out OpenAI’s new AI keypad — which will be fun for some coders and slightly mystifying to everyone else
items.summary:
OpenAI introduced Micro, its first hardware product, a compact keypad designed to work with ChatGPT and its coding tool Codex. Developed with keyboard designer Work Louder, Micro features customizable keys and a voice dictation button, aiming to enhance productivity for ChatGPT power users and coders. The device connects via Bluetooth or USB and allows users to assign specific tasks or projects to keys, with color-coded indicators for status.

Despite its sturdy build and sleek Apple-like packaging, Micro has received mixed reactions, especially from hardcore coders who question its value compared to traditional keyboards and cheaper alternatives. The $230 price point and learning curve have been points of criticism, though some users find it enjoyable once configured. OpenAI's broader hardware ambitions face legal challenges following a lawsuit from Apple alleging trade theft, leaving Micro as the company's current tangible offering in the hardware space.

items.title: Parody site OverpAId offers AI CEO replacement highlighting CEO-to-worker pay disparity amid AI automation debates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: New Parody Site Threatens to Replace CEOs With AI for Tiny Fraction of Their Bloated Salaries
items.summary:
A new parody website called OverpAId humorously claims to replace corporate CEOs with AI that performs executive tasks at a fraction of their salaries, spotlighting the growing CEO-to-worker pay gap. The site features satirical tools like jargon bingo and an ROI calculator to emphasize the disparity, noting that average CEO pay is about 290 times that of typical workers at large public companies.

While the site is satirical, it reflects real concerns about rising executive compensation outpacing worker wages and the potential impact of AI automation on labor. The project critiques the notion that high CEO pay benefits all employees, suggesting that the promised trickle-down effect has not materialized.

items.title: Alcorn State professor uses hidden white font prompt to catch 32 of 35 students cheating with AI on Industrial Revolution midterm [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Professor Hides White Font in Midterm, Catches Students Using AI in the Stupidest Way Possible
items.summary:
Jason Gibson, a history professor at Alcorn State University, concealed a prompt in white font instructing AI to generate nonsense in his midterm exam instructions. Thirty-two of his 35 students used AI to produce their entire responses without proofreading, resulting in failing grades due to irrelevant content about Madagascar inserted by the AI.

Gibson shared examples of the nonsensical AI-generated answers and emphasized that his goal was not to humiliate students but to uphold academic integrity. He explained the detection method to the students and allowed them to contest their grades, with only two doing so. This incident reflects broader challenges educators face with AI-assisted cheating, as institutions nationwide seek ways to maintain academic standards amid increasing AI use.

Thirty-two of his 35 students used AI to produce their entire responses without proofreading, resulting in failing grades due to irrelevant content about Madagascar inserted by the AI.

Gibson shared examples of the nonsensical AI-generated answers and emphasized that his goal was not to humiliate students but to uphold academic integrity. He explained the detection method to the students and allowed them to contest their grades, with only two doing so. This incident reflects broader challenges educators face with AI-assisted cheating, as institutions nationwide seek ways to maintain academic standards amid increasing AI use.

items.summary:
Prentis, an AI research lab launched in April by Reid Hoffman, Mark Pincus, and Ritankar Das, is negotiating a $100 million funding round at a $1 billion valuation. The company focuses on developing AI agents that automate routine office workflows by controlling computers, aiming to reduce manual tasks in industries like healthcare and manufacturing.

Prentis claims its Hive-32B model outperforms competitors such as OpenAI's GPT-5.4 and Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6 on benchmarks measuring task completion and interface navigation, while operating at a lower cost. The startup has secured contracts worth up to $50 million and projects an estimated $75 million annualized run rate by Q3 2026, though these figures are performance-dependent and not recognized revenue. The market for AI agents automating computer use is competitive, with other players like Anthropic and OpenAI also developing similar technologies.

items.title: Anthropic launches Opus 5 focusing on token efficiency with modest performance gains and lower costs compared to Fable and GPT-5.6-Sol [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic's Opus 5 is about token efficiency, not a capability leap
items.summary:
Anthropic released Opus 5, an update to its AI model popular for coding and software development, emphasizing token efficiency rather than a major capability leap. Opus 5 performs similarly or slightly better than Anthropic's Fable and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol on coding benchmarks, while costing less than Fable. The model lacks advanced cybersecurity training, resulting in weaker vulnerability exploitation compared to Mythos 5 and Fable, but it avoids some of Fable's data retention policies.

Opus 5 maintains pricing at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, cheaper than Fable but facing competition from models like China's Kimi K3 priced at $15 per million output tokens. Industry trends show growing interest in model routers that select AI models based on task complexity to optimize costs, highlighting the importance for companies like Anthropic to reduce token costs or improve performance to retain users amid rising adoption of smaller or open-weight models for less demanding tasks.
